# Unit 2: Geometrical and conformational isomerism, atropisomerism, stereospecific and stereoselective reactions

Unit 1 dealt with stereoisomers that arise from a stereocentre. This unit covers the other kinds: isomers caused by restricted rotation about a double bond or in a ring (geometrical isomers), shapes that interconvert by rotation about single bonds (conformations), chirality caused by hindered rotation in biphenyls (atropisomerism), and how the stereochemistry of reactions is described.

## 2.1 Geometrical isomerism

**Geometrical (cis–trans) isomers** are diastereomers that differ in the arrangement of groups on either side of a bond or ring about which free rotation is not possible.

**Why it happens.** In a C=C double bond the π bond is formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals above and below the plane. Turning one carbon would break this overlap, which needs much more energy than is available at room temperature. So groups are locked on one side or the other.

**Conditions for geometrical isomerism**

1. There must be restricted rotation: a C=C, C=N or N=N double bond, or a ring.
2. **Each** carbon of the double bond must carry two **different** groups. Abc=Cab type: isomers possible. If either carbon carries two identical groups (CH2=CHCl, (CH3)2C=CHCH3), there is no geometrical isomerism.

**Types of compounds showing it**

| System | Example |
| --- | --- |
| C=C | 2-butene, maleic and fumaric acids, cinnamic acid, stilbene |
| C=N | oximes of aldehydes and unsymmetrical ketones (benzaldoxime), hydrazones, imines |
| N=N | azobenzene |
| Rings | cis- and trans-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane; cis- and trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane |

## 2.2 Nomenclature of geometrical isomers

### Cis–trans system

Used when the two carbons carry a pair of similar groups.

- **cis**: similar groups on the **same** side.
- **trans**: similar groups on **opposite** sides.

```text
   H3C       CH3            H3C       H
      \     /                  \     /
       C = C                    C = C
      /     \                  /     \
     H       H                H       CH3
   cis-2-butene              trans-2-butene

   HOOC      COOH            HOOC      H
      \     /                  \     /
       C = C                    C = C
      /     \                  /     \
     H       H                H       COOH
   maleic acid (cis)         fumaric acid (trans)
```

Limitation: cis/trans fails when all four groups are different (for example BrClC=CHF), because there is no "similar" pair.

### E–Z system

Works for every alkene.

1. Rank the two groups on **each** carbon separately by the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog sequence rules (Unit 1).
2. If the two higher-priority groups are on the **same** side → **Z** (zusammen, together).
3. If on **opposite** sides → **E** (entgegen, opposite).

Example: 1-bromo-1-chloro-2-fluoroethene. On C-1, Br > Cl; on C-2, F > H. If Br and F are on the same side → (Z); opposite → (E).

Caution: cis is not always Z. In 2-chloro-2-butene type compounds, the priority order can make a "cis" arrangement of methyl groups E.

### Syn–anti system (oximes and C=N compounds)

The nitrogen of an oxime carries –OH and a lone pair.

- **Aldoximes** (RCH=NOH): **syn** when H and OH are on the same side; **anti** when they are on opposite sides. (Older books used the aryl group instead of H as the reference, so always state which convention you use.)
- **Ketoximes** (RR'C=NOH): the name names the group the OH is near, for example syn-phenyl methyl ketoxime means OH is on the side of the phenyl group.
- The E/Z system is now preferred for oximes as well.

## 2.3 Properties of geometrical isomers

| Property | cis isomer | trans isomer | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stability, heat of hydrogenation and combustion | Less stable; higher heats | More stable | Bulky groups crowd each other on the same side |
| Melting point | Lower | Higher | trans packs better in the crystal |
| Dipole moment | Higher (cis-1,2-dichloroethene about 1.9 D) | Zero or low (trans-1,2-dichloroethene 0 D) | Bond dipoles add in cis and cancel in trans |
| Boiling point | Usually higher | Usually lower | Higher polarity of cis |
| Solubility in water | Higher | Lower | Higher polarity |
| Density and refractive index | Usually higher | Usually lower | — |

Maleic acid melts at about 130–135 °C and is very soluble in water; fumaric acid melts near 287 °C (in a sealed tube) and is much less soluble.

## 2.4 Methods of determining the configuration of geometrical isomers

### A. Physical methods

1. **Dipole moment** — for symmetrical alkenes Xab=Cab, the isomer with the higher dipole moment is cis; trans has a zero or nearly zero value.
2. **Melting point and solubility** — the higher-melting, less soluble isomer is usually trans.
3. **Heat of combustion or hydrogenation** — the isomer releasing more heat (less stable) is usually cis.
4. **UV spectroscopy** — the trans isomer of a conjugated system such as stilbene is more planar, so it absorbs at a longer wavelength and with higher intensity than the cis isomer.
5. **IR spectroscopy** — trans-disubstituted alkenes show a strong C–H out-of-plane bending band near 965 cm⁻¹; cis-disubstituted alkenes absorb at lower frequency (roughly 675–730 cm⁻¹).
6. **NMR spectroscopy** — the coupling constant between the two vinylic hydrogens is larger for trans (about 12–18 Hz) than for cis (about 6–12 Hz).
7. **X-ray crystallography** — gives the full three-dimensional arrangement directly.

### B. Chemical methods

1. **Formation of a cyclic compound** — groups that react with each other to form a ring must be close together, which is possible only in the cis isomer. Maleic acid loses water on heating to give maleic anhydride; fumaric acid cannot form an anhydride directly (on strong heating it first converts to maleic anhydride). So maleic acid is cis.
2. **Formation from a ring compound** — opening a ring by a reaction that does not touch the double bond gives a cis product. Oxidation of benzene or quinone giving maleic acid supports its cis structure.
3. **Stereospecific addition reactions** — cold dilute alkaline KMnO4 adds two –OH groups to the same face (syn addition). Maleic acid gives meso-tartaric acid, while fumaric acid gives (±)-tartaric acid. Since the product's configuration is known, the starting alkene's configuration follows.
4. **Correlation with a compound of known configuration** — converting the alkene, without disturbing the double bond, into or from a compound whose configuration is already known.

### C. Configuration of oximes

- **Ketoximes — Beckmann rearrangement.** In acid (PCl5 or conc. H2SO4) the group **anti** to the –OH migrates to nitrogen (Unit 5). The amide formed shows which group was anti. For example, if acetophenone oxime gives acetanilide (CH3CONHC6H5), the phenyl group was anti to the OH.
- **Aldoximes — elimination test.** On treatment with acetic anhydride and then base, the isomer in which H and OH are trans to each other loses acetic acid easily and gives a nitrile (anti elimination); the other isomer gives back the oxime.

## 2.5 Conformational isomerism

**Conformations (conformers, rotamers)** are different spatial arrangements of a molecule produced by rotation about single (σ) bonds. They interconvert rapidly at room temperature and usually cannot be isolated. **Conformational analysis** studies their energies and populations.

**Ways of drawing them**

- **Sawhorse projection** — the C–C bond is drawn diagonally in perspective.
- **Newman projection** — looking straight down the C–C bond: the front carbon is a point where three bonds meet; the rear carbon is a circle with three bonds coming from its edge.

**Strains that raise energy**

| Strain | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| Torsional strain | Repulsion between bonding electron pairs in eclipsed bonds |
| Steric (van der Waals) strain | Bulky groups forced closer than their van der Waals radii allow |
| Angle strain | Bond angles forced away from the ideal (109.5° for sp3 carbon) |

### Ethane

```text
 Newman projection, looking down the C1–C2 bond
 (front C = centre point, rear C = circle)

 STAGGERED: rear H's sit exactly between the front H's
            H–C–C–H dihedral angle 60°  → lowest energy
 ECLIPSED : rear H's sit directly behind the front H's
            H–C–C–H dihedral angle 0°   → highest energy

 0° ──► 60° ──► 120° ──► 180° ──► 240° ──► 300° ──► 360°
 ecl.   stag.   ecl.     stag.    ecl.     stag.    ecl.
```

- Rotating one carbon through 360° passes through three staggered and three eclipsed forms.
- The eclipsed form is about **12 kJ/mol (about 2.9 kcal/mol)** higher than the staggered form, entirely due to torsional strain. This barrier is small, so rotation is fast at room temperature; ethane is almost always found staggered.

### n-Butane (rotation about C2–C3)

| Conformation | CH3–CH3 dihedral angle | Relative energy (approx.) | Comment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Anti (staggered) | 180° | 0 (most stable) | Methyls as far apart as possible |
| Gauche (staggered) | 60° | about 3.8 kJ/mol | Steric strain between methyls |
| Eclipsed (CH3 eclipses H) | 120° | about 16 kJ/mol | Torsional + some steric strain |
| Fully eclipsed (syn) | 0° | about 19 kJ/mol or more (least stable) | Methyl eclipses methyl |

Stability order: **anti > gauche > eclipsed > fully eclipsed**. At room temperature most butane molecules are in the anti form, with a smaller fraction gauche.

```text
 Energy
   ▲      fully                         fully
   │     eclipsed                      eclipsed
   │       /\        eclipsed  eclipsed  /\
   │      /  \         /\        /\     /  \
   │     /    \ gauche/  \ anti /  \gauche  \
   │____/      \_/\__/    \_/\_/    \_/\_____\___► rotation 0° → 360°
```

### Cyclohexane

Cyclohexane is not flat. A flat hexagon would have 120° angles (angle strain) and all bonds eclipsed. Puckering removes both problems.

**Conformations and approximate energies above the chair**

| Conformation | Energy (approx.) | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chair | 0 (most stable) | All C–C–C angles about 111°, all neighbouring C–H bonds staggered — almost strain-free |
| Twist-boat (skew-boat) | about 23 kJ/mol | Partly relieves the boat's strains; a true energy minimum but rarely populated |
| Boat | about 29 kJ/mol | Four pairs of eclipsed bonds and a "flagpole" clash between the two hydrogens pointing up at C-1 and C-4 |
| Half-chair | about 45 kJ/mol | Highest point on the path from chair to twist-boat (transition state) |

At room temperature over 99.9% of cyclohexane molecules are in the chair form.

```text
 CHAIR: carbons 1 and 4 point to opposite sides of the mean plane
        (one "up", one "down") → all bonds staggered, no flagpole clash
 BOAT : carbons 1 and 4 both point to the same side
        → the two inner ("flagpole") H's on C-1 and C-4 clash,
          and the C2–C3 and C5–C6 bonds are eclipsed

 chair ⇌ half-chair ⇌ twist-boat ⇌ boat ⇌ twist-boat ⇌ half-chair ⇌ other chair
```

**Axial and equatorial bonds.** Each carbon of the chair has one **axial** bond (parallel to the ring axis, alternately up and down) and one **equatorial** bond (roughly along the "equator" of the ring). There are 6 axial and 6 equatorial hydrogens.

**Ring flipping.** The chair rapidly flips into the other chair; every axial bond becomes equatorial and vice versa.

**Monosubstituted cyclohexanes.** A substituent prefers the **equatorial** position. In the axial position it clashes with the two axial hydrogens on the same side, three carbons away (**1,3-diaxial interactions**, which are gauche-butane-like interactions). For methylcyclohexane about 95% of molecules have the methyl equatorial at room temperature. A very bulky group such as tert-butyl stays equatorial almost completely and "locks" the ring.

**Disubstituted cyclohexanes.** The most stable conformation is the one with the larger number of (and the bulkier) groups equatorial. trans-1,4-Dimethylcyclohexane can place both methyls equatorial and is more stable than the cis isomer, which must have one axial.

## 2.6 Stereoisomerism in biphenyl compounds (atropisomerism)

Biphenyl normally rotates freely about the single bond joining the two rings. If **bulky groups occupy the ortho positions** (2, 2', 6 and 6'), they bump into each other and rotation is blocked. The two rings are then held roughly perpendicular to each other.

**Atropisomers** are stereoisomers that can be isolated because rotation about a single bond is hindered (Greek *atropos*, "not turning"). The chirality is due to a **chiral axis**, not a stereocentre.

**Conditions for optical activity in biphenyls**

1. The ortho substituents must be large enough to prevent rotation at the working temperature (for example –NO2, –COOH, –Br, –I, –SO3H). Small groups such as –F or –OCH3 often allow slow rotation and the forms racemise.
2. **Each ring must be unsymmetrically substituted**: the two ortho groups on the same ring must be different (a ≠ b on one ring and c ≠ d on the other). If either ring carries two identical ortho groups, the molecule has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive.

```text
       a           c          a ≠ b  and  c ≠ d
        \         /           rings held perpendicular
    ring A ──── ring B        → non-superimposable mirror images
        /         \
       b           d
 Example: 6,6'-dinitrobiphenyl-2,2'-dicarboxylic acid (6,6'-dinitrodiphenic acid)
 was resolved into optically active forms.
```

Atropisomers interconvert if heated enough to overcome the barrier; the higher the barrier, the more stable the separate forms. Related cases of axial chirality occur in suitably substituted allenes (abC=C=Cab) and spiranes. Atropisomerism is relevant to some modern drugs whose hindered biaryl bonds give separable isomers with different activity.

## 2.7 Stereospecific and stereoselective reactions

**Stereoselective reaction**: one stereoisomer of the product is formed **in preference** to others, when more than one could form. Selectivity can be partial.

- Dehydrohalogenation of 2-bromobutane with alcoholic KOH gives more trans-2-butene than cis-2-butene.
- Reduction of 4-tert-butylcyclohexanone with LiAlH4 gives mainly the trans alcohol (OH equatorial).
- Asymmetric synthesis (Unit 1) is enantioselective.

**Stereospecific reaction**: stereoisomeric starting materials give **stereoisomerically different** products — the mechanism decides the stereochemistry.

| Reaction | Starting isomer | Product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Br2 addition (anti addition, through a bromonium ion) | cis-2-butene | (±)-2,3-dibromobutane |
| | trans-2-butene | meso-2,3-dibromobutane |
| Cold dilute alkaline KMnO4 or OsO4 (syn addition) | cis-2-butene | meso-2,3-butanediol |
| | trans-2-butene | (±)-2,3-butanediol |
| | maleic acid | meso-tartaric acid |
| | fumaric acid | (±)-tartaric acid |
| SN2 substitution | (R) halide | (S) product (inversion) |
| E2 elimination | needs H and leaving group anti-periplanar; different diastereomers give different alkene isomers |
| Catalytic hydrogenation of alkynes (Lindlar catalyst) vs Na in liquid NH3 | same alkyne | cis-alkene vs trans-alkene |

**Relationship:** every stereospecific reaction is stereoselective, but a stereoselective reaction need not be stereospecific.

**Mechanism of anti addition of bromine (why cis gives racemate):**

```text
 cis-2-butene + Br2 → cyclic bromonium ion (Br bridges both carbons from one face)
 Br⁻ attacks from the opposite face, at either carbon (50:50)
 → (2R,3R) + (2S,3S) = racemic 2,3-dibromobutane
 The same steps on trans-2-butene give (2R,3S) = meso
```

## Remember

- Geometrical isomerism needs restricted rotation **and** two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon.
- cis/trans uses similar groups; E/Z uses CIP priority on each carbon; syn/anti for oximes.
- trans: higher melting point, more stable, lower dipole; cis: higher dipole, more soluble, forms cyclic anhydride (maleic acid).
- Determine configuration by dipole moment, melting point, IR (trans ~965 cm⁻¹), NMR J (trans larger), ring formation, syn addition products, Beckmann rearrangement (anti group migrates).
- Ethane: staggered more stable by about 12 kJ/mol. Butane: anti > gauche > eclipsed > fully eclipsed.
- Cyclohexane: chair > twist-boat > boat > half-chair; substituents prefer equatorial (1,3-diaxial strain).
- Biphenyl optical activity: bulky ortho groups and each ring unsymmetrically substituted; chiral axis, not a stereocentre.
- Stereospecific: product stereochemistry fixed by the starting isomer (Br2 to cis-2-butene → racemate, to trans → meso). Stereoselective: one product preferred.

# Unit 3: Heterocyclic compounds — nomenclature, classification, pyrrole, furan and thiophene

**Heterocyclic compounds** are cyclic compounds in which the ring contains at least one atom other than carbon. The most common hetero atoms are nitrogen, oxygen and sulphur. More than half of all known drugs contain a heterocyclic ring, along with vitamins, nucleic acid bases, alkaloids, antibiotics and pigments such as haem and chlorophyll. This unit covers naming and classifying heterocycles and then the three five-membered aromatic rings with one hetero atom: pyrrole, furan and thiophene.

## 3.1 Classification of heterocyclic compounds

| Basis | Classes | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ring size | Three-, four-, five-, six-, seven-membered | oxirane, azetidine, pyrrole, pyridine, azepine |
| Number of hetero atoms | One, two or more | furan (1); imidazole (2); 1,2,4-triazole (3) |
| Kind of hetero atom | N, O, S or a mixture | pyrrole (N); oxazole (N, O); thiazole (N, S) |
| Degree of unsaturation | Aromatic; partly saturated; fully saturated (behave like ordinary amines, ethers, sulphides) | pyrrole; 3-pyrroline; pyrrolidine |
| Ring fusion | Monocyclic; fused with benzene; fused with another heterocycle | pyridine; quinoline, indole; purine, pteridine |
| Electron distribution (aromatic rings) | π-excessive (five-membered, electron-rich); π-deficient (six-membered with N, electron-poor) | pyrrole, furan, thiophene; pyridine, pyrimidine |

## 3.2 Nomenclature

Three systems are used.

### (a) Trivial (common) names

Most important heterocycles keep old names, which IUPAC accepts: pyrrole, furan, thiophene, pyridine, quinoline, isoquinoline, indole, purine, pyrimidine, imidazole. They must simply be learnt.

### (b) Hantzsch–Widman (systematic) names

Built from three parts: **prefix(es) for the hetero atoms + stem for ring size and saturation**.

**Prefixes** (in order of priority, highest first):

| Hetero atom | Prefix |
| --- | --- |
| Oxygen | oxa- |
| Sulphur | thia- |
| Nitrogen | aza- |

The final "a" is dropped before a vowel (oxa + ole = oxole).

**Stems (for rings with up to five members)**

| Ring size | Unsaturated (max. non-cumulative double bonds) | Saturated, containing N | Saturated, without N |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | -irine (N) / -irene | -iridine | -irane |
| 4 | -ete | -etidine | -etane |
| 5 | -ole | -olidine | -olane |

For six-membered rings containing nitrogen, the unsaturated stem is **-ine** (azine = pyridine, 1,3-diazine = pyrimidine) and the saturated one is **-inane** (azinane = piperidine).

**Examples**

| Structure | Hantzsch–Widman name | Common name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Three-membered ring, one O, saturated | oxirane | ethylene oxide |
| Three-membered ring, one N, saturated | aziridine | ethyleneimine |
| Four-membered ring, one N, saturated | azetidine | — (the β-lactam ring of penicillins is azetidin-2-one) |
| Five-membered, one O, unsaturated | oxole | furan |
| Five-membered, one S, unsaturated | thiole | thiophene |
| Five-membered, one N, unsaturated | azole | pyrrole |
| Five-membered, one O, saturated | oxolane | tetrahydrofuran (THF) |
| Five-membered, N at 1 and 3 | 1,3-diazole | imidazole |
| Five-membered, O at 1 and N at 3 | 1,3-oxazole | oxazole |
| Five-membered, S at 1 and N at 3 | 1,3-thiazole | thiazole |

**Numbering rules**

1. Start at the hetero atom of highest priority (O > S > N) and give it number 1.
2. Go round the ring so that the other hetero atoms get the lowest possible numbers.
3. Substituents are then numbered by the same scheme (2-methylfuran, 3-bromothiophene).
4. Greek letters are also used for five-membered rings: positions next to the hetero atom (2 and 5) are **α**; positions 3 and 4 are **β**.

```text
            β     β
            4 ─── 3
           /       \
      α   5         2   α        X = NH (pyrrole), O (furan), S (thiophene)
           \       /
              X 1
```

### (c) Replacement nomenclature

The heterocycle is named as the carbocycle with "aza", "oxa" or "thia" showing which carbon is replaced. Quinoline = 1-azanaphthalene; isoquinoline = 2-azanaphthalene; acridine relates to anthracene.

### Fused ring names

Fused systems are named by joining a prefix (benzo-, pyrido-, imidazo-) to the base ring and giving letters (a, b, c…) for the bond of fusion: indole = benzo[b]pyrrole; quinoline = benzo[b]pyridine; isoquinoline = benzo[c]pyridine.

## 3.3 Aromaticity of pyrrole, furan and thiophene

Each of these is a flat five-membered ring. The four carbons are sp2 hybridised and each gives one p electron. The hetero atom is also sp2 and gives **two** electrons (one lone pair) into the p orbital perpendicular to the ring. This makes **6 π electrons** in a cyclic, planar, fully conjugated system — Hückel's rule (4n + 2, n = 1) is obeyed, so the rings are aromatic.

```text
   p orbitals above and below the ring plane
     ○   ○   ○   ○   ○       4 C × 1 e  +  heteroatom × 2 e  =  6 π electrons
     │   │   │   │   │
   ──C───C───C───C───X──     (in furan and thiophene the second lone pair of
     │   │   │   │   │        O or S lies in the ring plane and is not part
     ○   ○   ○   ○   ○        of the aromatic sextet)
```

Because the hetero atom pushes its lone pair into the ring, the ring carbons carry more electron density than benzene carbons. These rings are called **π-excessive** and react with electrophiles much faster than benzene.

**Relative aromaticity.** Aromatic character depends on how easily the hetero atom shares its lone pair. Oxygen is the most electronegative and holds its electrons tightly, so furan is the least aromatic. Sulphur is less electronegative and its larger orbitals overlap acceptably, so thiophene is the most aromatic of the three. Approximate resonance energies commonly quoted:

| Compound | Resonance energy (approx.) |
| --- | --- |
| Benzene | 150 kJ/mol (36 kcal/mol) |
| Thiophene | 122 kJ/mol (29 kcal/mol) |
| Pyrrole | 88 kJ/mol (21 kcal/mol) |
| Furan | 67 kJ/mol (16 kcal/mol) |

**Order of aromaticity: benzene > thiophene > pyrrole > furan.**

Furan's low aromaticity shows in its chemistry: it adds reagents (it takes part in Diels–Alder reactions as a diene), opens easily in acid, and behaves partly like a diene ether.

**Relative reactivity towards electrophiles** is roughly the reverse: **pyrrole > furan > thiophene > benzene**. Nitrogen is the best electron donor, so the intermediate cation from pyrrole is best stabilised.

**Why substitution occurs at C-2 (α).** Attack at C-2 gives a cation stabilised by three resonance structures (positive charge on C-3, C-5 and the hetero atom). Attack at C-3 gives only two (charge on C-2 and the hetero atom). The more stable intermediate forms faster, so α-substitution dominates. If both α positions are occupied, substitution goes to β.

## 3.4 Pyrrole

Pyrrole (C4H5N) is a colourless liquid (bp about 130 °C) that darkens in air. It occurs in coal tar and bone oil. The pyrrole ring is part of porphyrins (haem, chlorophyll), vitamin B12 (corrin ring), bile pigments, and the amino acids proline and hydroxyproline (as the saturated pyrrolidine ring).

### Synthesis of pyrrole

1. **Paal–Knorr synthesis** — a 1,4-dicarbonyl compound is heated with ammonia (or a primary amine) to give a pyrrole. Hexane-2,5-dione (acetonylacetone) + NH3 → 2,5-dimethylpyrrole + 2 H2O; with methylamine the product is 1,2,5-trimethylpyrrole.

```text
  CH3–CO–CH2–CH2–CO–CH3  +  NH3   ──heat──►   2,5-dimethylpyrrole  +  2 H2O
     hexane-2,5-dione                         (ring closed by N between the two C=O carbons)
```

2. **From succinimide** — distilling succinimide with zinc dust reduces it to pyrrole.
3. **From ammonium mucate** — dry distillation of the ammonium salt of mucic acid (with glycerol) gives pyrrole.
4. **From furan (industrial)** — furan, ammonia and steam passed over heated alumina give pyrrole (the O is replaced by NH).
5. **Knorr pyrrole synthesis** — an α-aminoketone condenses with a β-ketoester (or other ketone with an active CH2) to give a substituted pyrrole. α-Aminoketones are unstable, so they are made in the flask by reducing an oximino ketone with zinc and acetic acid.
6. **Hantzsch pyrrole synthesis** — a β-ketoester, an α-haloketone and ammonia (or a primary amine) give a substituted pyrrole.

### Basicity and acidity of pyrrole

- Pyrrole is an **extremely weak base** (pKa of its conjugate acid about −3.8, compared with about 11 for pyrrolidine). The nitrogen lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet; using it to take a proton would destroy aromaticity. When pyrrole is protonated by strong acid, the proton actually adds to **C-2**, not N.
- Pyrrole is a **weak acid** (N–H pKa about 17). It reacts with potassium metal or solid KOH to give potassium pyrrolide, and with Grignard reagents to give pyrrylmagnesium halide. The anion is stabilised because the negative charge is spread over the aromatic ring.
- In strong acids pyrrole **polymerises** (protonated pyrrole is attacked by neutral pyrrole), giving a red resin. So strongly acidic reagents (conc. HNO3/H2SO4) cannot be used directly.

### Reactions of pyrrole

**Electrophilic substitution (mostly at C-2), under mild, non-acidic conditions:**

| Reaction | Reagent | Product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nitration | Acetyl nitrate (HNO3 + acetic anhydride) at low temperature | 2-Nitropyrrole |
| Sulphonation | Pyridine–SO3 complex | Pyrrole-2-sulphonic acid |
| Halogenation | I2 in KI; SO2Cl2 | 2,3,4,5-Tetraiodopyrrole (iodol, once an antiseptic); tetrachloropyrrole — halogenation is hard to stop at one atom |
| Acylation | Acetic anhydride on heating (no catalyst needed) | 2-Acetylpyrrole |
| Formylation | DMF + POCl3 (Vilsmeier–Haack) | Pyrrole-2-carbaldehyde |
| Reimer–Tiemann | CHCl3 + KOH | Pyrrole-2-carbaldehyde, with some 3-chloropyridine from ring expansion |
| Mannich | HCHO + dimethylamine | 2-(Dimethylaminomethyl)pyrrole |
| Diazo coupling | Benzenediazonium chloride | 2-Phenylazopyrrole (coloured) |

**Reactions at nitrogen** — potassium pyrrolide reacts with CH3I to give N-methylpyrrole and with acyl chlorides to give N-acylpyrroles.

**Reduction**
- Zinc and acetic acid → 3-pyrroline (2,5-dihydropyrrole).
- H2 / Ni or Pt (heat) → pyrrolidine (a strong secondary amine base).

**Oxidation** — with chromium trioxide pyrrole gives maleimide.

**Ring expansion** — as noted, the Reimer–Tiemann conditions (dichlorocarbene) can give 3-chloropyridine.

### Medicinal uses of pyrrole and its derivatives

| Compound | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Haem (porphyrin of four pyrroles) | Oxygen transport in haemoglobin |
| Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin, corrin ring) | Treatment of pernicious anaemia |
| Atorvastatin | Lowers cholesterol (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor) |
| Tolmetin, ketorolac | NSAIDs (ketorolac has a fused pyrrolizine ring) |
| Sunitinib | Anticancer (kinase inhibitor) |
| Povidone (polyvinylpyrrolidone) | Pharmaceutical binder; povidone-iodine antiseptic |
| Piracetam (pyrrolidone) | Nootropic |

## 3.5 Furan

Furan (C4H4O) is a colourless volatile liquid (bp about 31 °C). Its name comes from Latin *furfur* (bran), because its aldehyde, furfural, is obtained from bran.

### Synthesis of furan

1. **From pentosans (industrial)** — oat husks, corn cobs or bran (rich in pentosans) are heated with dilute H2SO4 or HCl. The pentoses formed lose water to give **furfural** (furan-2-carbaldehyde). Furfural is decarbonylated (CO removed) by passing its vapour with steam over a heated catalyst (for example ZnO–Cr2O3, or palladium) to give furan.

```text
 pentosans ──H3O+──► pentoses (C5H10O5) ──(−3 H2O)──► furfural ──(−CO, catalyst)──► furan
```

2. **From mucic acid** — dry distillation of mucic acid gives furan-2-carboxylic acid (pyromucic acid), which loses CO2 on heating to give furan.
3. **Paal–Knorr synthesis** — a 1,4-dicarbonyl compound is heated with a dehydrating agent (P2O5, H2SO4 or ZnCl2): hexane-2,5-dione → 2,5-dimethylfuran.
4. **Feist–Bénary synthesis** — an α-haloketone condenses with a β-ketoester in the presence of a base such as pyridine or ammonia, giving a substituted furan.

### Reactions of furan

Furan is very reactive and acid-sensitive, so mild reagents are used. Substitution occurs at C-2.

| Reaction | Reagent | Product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nitration | Acetyl nitrate at low temperature | 2-Nitrofuran |
| Sulphonation | Pyridine–SO3 | Furan-2-sulphonic acid |
| Bromination | Bromine in dioxane at low temperature | 2-Bromofuran |
| Acylation | Acetic anhydride with a mild Lewis acid (BF3) | 2-Acetylfuran |
| Formylation | Vilsmeier–Haack (DMF/POCl3) | Furfural |

**Addition reactions** (reflect low aromaticity):

- **Diels–Alder reaction** — furan acts as a diene with maleic anhydride, giving an oxygen-bridged adduct.
- **Catalytic hydrogenation** (H2/Ni) → **tetrahydrofuran (THF)**, a common solvent.
- **Ring opening** — aqueous acid opens the ring to give 1,4-dicarbonyl compounds (the reverse of the Paal–Knorr reaction).

### Medicinal uses of furan and its derivatives

| Compound | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Nitrofurantoin | Urinary tract antiseptic |
| Nitrofurazone | Topical antibacterial for wounds and burns |
| Furazolidone | Antibacterial and antiprotozoal (diarrhoea, giardiasis) |
| Ranitidine | H2 receptor antagonist for peptic ulcer |
| Furosemide | Loop diuretic (contains a furfurylamino group) |
| Dantrolene | Skeletal muscle relaxant |
| Tetrahydrofuran | Solvent in drug synthesis |

## 3.6 Thiophene

Thiophene (C4H4S) is a colourless liquid (bp about 84 °C) with a smell like benzene. It occurs in coal-tar benzene, from which it is hard to separate by distillation because the boiling points are close. Victor Meyer discovered it when a sample of "benzene" gave a blue colour with isatin and conc. H2SO4 (the **indophenin test**), while pure benzene did not.

**Removal of thiophene from benzene**: shake the benzene with conc. H2SO4 at room temperature. Thiophene sulphonates much faster than benzene and passes into the acid layer as thiophene-2-sulphonic acid.

### Synthesis of thiophene

1. **Industrial** — n-butane (or butenes, butadiene) heated with sulphur at high temperature (around 560 °C).
2. **Volhard–Erdmann synthesis** — heating sodium succinate with phosphorus trisulphide (P2S3) gives thiophene.
3. **Paal–Knorr synthesis** — a 1,4-dicarbonyl compound heated with phosphorus pentasulphide (P2S5, also written P4S10): hexane-2,5-dione → 2,5-dimethylthiophene.
4. **From acetylene** — acetylene and hydrogen sulphide passed over heated alumina.
5. **Hinsberg synthesis** — a 1,2-dicarbonyl compound condenses with diethyl thiodiacetate in base, giving a thiophenedicarboxylic acid derivative.

### Reactions of thiophene

Thiophene is the most benzene-like of the three: it is stable to acids and can be sulphonated with conc. H2SO4. It still reacts faster than benzene, and at C-2.

| Reaction | Reagent | Product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nitration | HNO3 in acetic anhydride | 2-Nitrothiophene |
| Sulphonation | Conc. H2SO4 at room temperature | Thiophene-2-sulphonic acid |
| Halogenation | Br2 or Cl2 (fast; can give polyhalo products) | 2-Bromothiophene, 2,5-dibromothiophene |
| Acylation | Acetic anhydride with H3PO4, or acetyl chloride with SnCl4 | 2-Acetylthiophene |
| Chloromethylation | HCHO + HCl | 2-Chloromethylthiophene |
| Mercuration | HgCl2 with sodium acetate | 2-Chloromercurithiophene |

**Other reactions**

- **Desulphurisation with Raney nickel** — removes sulphur and saturates the chain, giving an alkane (thiophene → n-butane). This is used to make chains of known length from thiophene derivatives.
- **Reduction** — thiophene poisons ordinary hydrogenation catalysts; with large amounts of palladium it gives tetrahydrothiophene (thiolane). Biotin contains this saturated ring.
- **Oxidation** — peracids oxidise the sulphur to the sulphoxide and sulphone (thiophene 1,1-dioxide), which are no longer aromatic.

### Medicinal uses of thiophene and its derivatives

| Compound | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Clopidogrel, ticlopidine, prasugrel (thienopyridines) | Antiplatelet drugs |
| Tenoxicam | NSAID (oxicam with thiophene in place of benzene) |
| Ticarcillin, cefalotin | β-Lactam antibiotics with a thiophene side chain |
| Olanzapine (thienobenzodiazepine) | Antipsychotic |
| Duloxetine | Antidepressant (SNRI) |
| Tiotropium | Inhaled bronchodilator for COPD |
| Biotin (tetrahydrothiophene ring) | Vitamin |

**Bioisosterism.** A thiophene ring often replaces a benzene ring in drug design ("thiophene is a bioisostere of benzene") because its size, shape and electronic nature are similar; tenoxicam vs piroxicam is an example.

## 3.7 Comparison of the three rings

| Property | Pyrrole | Furan | Thiophene |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hetero atom | NH | O | S |
| Aromaticity | Intermediate | Least | Most (closest to benzene) |
| Reactivity to electrophiles | Highest | Intermediate | Lowest of the three, but more than benzene |
| Stability in acid | Polymerises | Ring opens | Stable |
| Preferred site of substitution | C-2 | C-2 | C-2 |
| Diels–Alder as diene | Poor | Good | Very poor |
| Paal–Knorr reagent with 1,4-diketone | NH3 or RNH2 | Acid / P2O5 | P2S5 |
| Main natural or industrial source | Coal tar, bone oil | Furfural (bran) | Coal-tar benzene; butane + S |

## Remember

- Hantzsch–Widman: oxa > thia > aza; 5-membered unsaturated "-ole", saturated with N "-olidine", without N "-olane"; number from the highest-priority hetero atom.
- Pyrrole, furan, thiophene: 6 π electrons, the hetero atom lone pair is in the sextet → π-excessive, attacked at C-2.
- Aromaticity: benzene > thiophene > pyrrole > furan. Reactivity to electrophiles: pyrrole > furan > thiophene > benzene.
- Pyrrole is almost non-basic (lone pair in the sextet; protonates on C-2) and weakly acidic at N–H (forms K salt).
- Paal–Knorr: 1,4-diketone + NH3 (pyrrole), + acid (furan), + P2S5 (thiophene).
- Furan from furfural (bran + acid, then decarbonylation); thiophene detected by the indophenin test and removed from benzene with conc. H2SO4.
- Use mild reagents: acetyl nitrate for nitration, pyridine–SO3 for sulphonation (except thiophene, which tolerates conc. H2SO4).
- Drugs: atorvastatin, ketorolac (pyrrole); nitrofurantoin, furosemide, ranitidine (furan); clopidogrel, tenoxicam, olanzapine (thiophene).

# Unit 4: Azoles, pyridine and fused rings, pyrimidine, purine and azepines

This unit continues heterocyclic chemistry with the rings that appear in the largest number of drugs: the five-membered rings with two hetero atoms (azoles), pyridine and the benzo-fused rings built on it, indole, and the six- and seven-membered rings with nitrogen. For each compound learn **one or two named syntheses, the key reactions with the position of attack, and two or three drugs**.

## 4.1 Two facts that explain most of this unit

**1. Pyridine-type nitrogen vs pyrrole-type nitrogen.**

| | Pyrrole-type N (–NH– in a five-membered ring) | Pyridine-type N (–N= in the ring) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lone pair | Part of the aromatic sextet | In an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, **not** part of the sextet |
| Basicity | Almost none | Basic (can take a proton without losing aromaticity) |
| Effect on ring | Pushes electrons in (π-excessive) | Pulls electrons out (π-deficient) |

The azoles contain **one of each**: imidazole, pyrazole, oxazole and thiazole all have a pyridine-type N.

**2. Electron-rich vs electron-poor rings.** Five-membered rings react with electrophiles easily. Six-membered rings with nitrogen (pyridine, pyrimidine) resist electrophiles but are attacked by **nucleophiles** at the positions ortho and para to nitrogen (C-2, C-4, C-6).

**Approximate basicity (pKa of the conjugate acid)**

| Compound | pKa (approx.) | Comment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Piperidine (saturated) | 11.1 | sp3 N, strong base |
| Imidazole | 7.0 | Cation stabilised by resonance over both N |
| Isoquinoline | 5.4 | |
| Pyridine | 5.2 | sp2 N |
| Quinoline | 4.9 | |
| Aniline (for comparison) | 4.6 | Lone pair delocalised into the benzene ring |
| Thiazole | 2.5 | |
| Pyrazole | 2.5 | Neighbouring N withdraws electrons |
| Pyrimidine | 1.3 | Second N withdraws electrons |
| Oxazole | 0.8 | O withdraws electrons |
| Pyrrole | about −3.8 | Lone pair in the sextet |

## 4.2 Pyrazole (1,2-diazole)

Five-membered ring with two adjacent nitrogens: N-1 (pyrrole-type, NH) and N-2 (pyridine-type). Colourless solid, weak base and weak acid. Like imidazole it shows **tautomerism**: the NH hydrogen moves between N-1 and N-2, so 3- and 5-substituted pyrazoles interconvert.

### Synthesis

1. **From 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds and hydrazine (Knorr-type)** — the most general method.

```text
 CH3–CO–CH2–CO–CH3  +  H2N–NH2   ──►   3,5-dimethylpyrazole  +  2 H2O
   acetylacetone        hydrazine        (both C=O groups condense with the two NH2 ends)
```

   With phenylhydrazine, N-phenylpyrazoles are obtained. Ethyl acetoacetate + phenylhydrazine gives a **pyrazolone**, the starting point for antipyrine (phenazone).

2. **From α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compounds and hydrazine** — gives a pyrazoline (dihydropyrazole), which is then oxidised to the pyrazole.
3. **From diazomethane and acetylene** — 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition gives pyrazole directly.

### Reactions

- **Electrophilic substitution at C-4** (the most electron-rich carbon): nitration (HNO3/H2SO4) → 4-nitropyrazole; sulphonation → pyrazole-4-sulphonic acid; bromination → 4-bromopyrazole.
- **N-alkylation and N-acylation** at the NH nitrogen.
- **Salt formation** with strong acids at N-2.
- **Stable to oxidation**; side chains can be oxidised to carboxylic acids. Reduction gives pyrazoline and then pyrazolidine.

### Medicinal uses

| Drug | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Antipyrine (phenazone), aminopyrine, metamizole (dipyrone) | Analgesic–antipyretics (pyrazolones) |
| Phenylbutazone, oxyphenbutazone | Anti-inflammatory (pyrazolidinediones) |
| Celecoxib | Selective COX-2 inhibitor |
| Sildenafil | PDE-5 inhibitor (pyrazolopyrimidinone) |
| Allopurinol | Gout (pyrazolo[3,4-d]pyrimidine, a purine isomer) |

## 4.3 Imidazole (1,3-diazole)

Nitrogens at 1 (NH) and 3 (=N–). Colourless solid with a high boiling point (about 256 °C) because molecules link by strong intermolecular N–H···N hydrogen bonds. It is **amphoteric**: a moderately strong base (pKa about 7) and a weak acid (NH pKa about 14.5). Its basicity near physiological pH is why the imidazole ring of histidine acts as a proton donor and acceptor in many enzymes.

Tautomerism makes positions 4 and 5 equivalent in the unsubstituted ring; a 4-substituted imidazole is often written 4(5)-substituted.

### Synthesis

1. **Debus–Radziszewski synthesis** — a 1,2-dicarbonyl compound, an aldehyde and ammonia condense together.

```text
 glyoxal (OHC–CHO) + formaldehyde (HCHO) + 2 NH3  ──►  imidazole + 3 H2O
 benzil + benzaldehyde + NH3 (as ammonium acetate)  ──►  2,4,5-triphenylimidazole
```

2. **From α-haloketones and formamide (Bredereck)** — heating an α-haloketone (or α-hydroxyketone) with formamide gives 4-substituted imidazoles.
3. **Marckwald synthesis** — an α-aminoketone (or α-aminoaldehyde acetal) reacts with potassium thiocyanate to give a 2-mercaptoimidazole; the –SH is then removed by oxidation (dilute HNO3) to give the imidazole.
4. **From o-phenylenediamine** — with formic acid or an aldehyde, it gives **benzimidazole**, the parent of a large drug family.

### Reactions

- **Basic reactions** — forms stable salts (imidazolium) with acids; reacts with alkyl halides at N-3 to give N-alkylimidazoles and then imidazolium salts.
- **N-Acylation** — gives N-acylimidazoles, which are reactive acylating agents; carbonyldiimidazole (CDI) is used to couple acids and amines in peptide and drug synthesis.
- **Electrophilic substitution at C-4/C-5**, needing stronger conditions than pyrrole: nitration (HNO3/H2SO4) → 4(5)-nitroimidazole (the core of metronidazole); bromination → 2,4,5-tribromoimidazole (substitution goes all the way).
- **Diazo coupling at C-2** with diazonium salts in alkaline solution.
- Resistant to oxidation and reduction.

### Medicinal uses

| Drug or compound | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Histidine, histamine | Amino acid; mediator of allergy and gastric acid secretion |
| Metronidazole, tinidazole, ornidazole | Nitroimidazoles: amoebiasis, giardiasis, trichomoniasis, anaerobic infections |
| Clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole | Azole antifungals |
| Cimetidine | H2 receptor antagonist |
| Albendazole, mebendazole | Benzimidazole anthelmintics |
| Omeprazole, pantoprazole | Benzimidazole proton pump inhibitors |
| Pilocarpine | Glaucoma (cholinergic) |
| Losartan | Angiotensin II receptor blocker |

## 4.4 Oxazole (1,3-oxazole)

Oxygen at 1 and pyridine-type nitrogen at 3. It is a weak base (pKa about 0.8) and is the least aromatic of the azoles because oxygen holds its lone pair tightly. Its isomer **isoxazole** (1,2-oxazole) has O and N next to each other.

### Synthesis

1. **Robinson–Gabriel synthesis** — an α-acylaminoketone (2-acylamino ketone) is cyclised by dehydrating agents such as conc. H2SO4, POCl3 or PCl5.

```text
 R–CO–CH2–NH–CO–R'   ──(conc. H2SO4 or POCl3, −H2O)──►   2,5-disubstituted oxazole
 α-acylaminoketone
```

2. **Fischer oxazole synthesis** — an aldehyde cyanohydrin and an aromatic aldehyde react in dry ether with dry HCl to give a 2,5-diaryloxazole.
3. **From α-haloketones and amides (Bredereck)** — an α-haloketone heated with formamide (or another amide) gives an oxazole.
4. **van Leusen synthesis** — an aldehyde and tosylmethyl isocyanide (TosMIC) with a base (K2CO3) give a 5-substituted oxazole.

### Reactions

- **Electrophilic substitution** is difficult (the ring is electron-poor); with activating groups it occurs at **C-5**, then C-4.
- **Deprotonation at C-2** with strong bases (butyllithium); the C-2 hydrogen is the most acidic.
- **Nucleophilic substitution at C-2** when a leaving group (e.g. Cl) is present.
- **Diels–Alder reaction as a diene** — oxazoles react with dienophiles to give pyridine derivatives. A 5-ethoxyoxazole with a suitable dienophile is the basis of an industrial route to **pyridoxine (vitamin B6)**.
- Ring opening by acids or bases.

### Medicinal uses

| Drug | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Oxaprozin | NSAID (oxazole) |
| Sulfamethoxazole | Sulphonamide antibacterial (isoxazole ring), with trimethoprim as co-trimoxazole |
| Cloxacillin, dicloxacillin, oxacillin | Penicillinase-resistant penicillins (isoxazolyl side chain) |
| Leflunomide | Rheumatoid arthritis (isoxazole) |
| Linezolid | Antibacterial (oxazolidinone, the saturated relative) |

## 4.5 Thiazole (1,3-thiazole)

Sulphur at 1 and pyridine-type nitrogen at 3. Weak base (pKa about 2.5), more aromatic than oxazole.

### Synthesis

1. **Hantzsch thiazole synthesis** — the most important. An α-haloketone condenses with a **thioamide**; with **thiourea** the product is a 2-aminothiazole.

```text
 CH3–CO–CH2Cl   +   CH3–CS–NH2     ──►   2,4-dimethylthiazole  + HCl + H2O
 chloroacetone      thioacetamide
 CH3–CO–CH2Cl   +   H2N–CS–NH2     ──►   2-amino-4-methylthiazole
                    thiourea
```

2. **Gabriel synthesis** — an α-acylaminoketone heated with phosphorus pentasulphide (P2S5) gives a thiazole (the sulphur analogue of the Robinson–Gabriel oxazole synthesis).
3. **Cook–Heilbron synthesis** — an α-aminonitrile reacts with carbon disulphide (or dithioacids, isothiocyanates) to give 5-aminothiazoles.

### Reactions

- **Electrophilic substitution at C-5** (the preferred site), easier when activated: 2-aminothiazole brominates and nitrates at C-5.
- **N-Alkylation** at N-3 gives **thiazolium salts**. The C-2 hydrogen of a thiazolium salt is acidic; removing it gives a reactive species that catalyses decarboxylation of α-keto acids. This is how **thiamine pyrophosphate** (vitamin B1 coenzyme) works in the body.
- **Deprotonation at C-2** with butyllithium; **nucleophilic substitution** of 2-halothiazoles.
- **Desulphurisation with Raney nickel** opens the ring.
- Thiazole is resistant to oxidation; reduction gives thiazoline and thiazolidine (the thiazolidine ring is fused to the β-lactam in penicillins).

## 4.6 Pyridine

Pyridine (C5H5N) is a colourless liquid (bp about 115 °C) with an unpleasant smell, obtained from coal tar (light oil) and bone oil. It is miscible with water and most organic solvents and is widely used as a basic solvent and catalyst (acylations).

**Structure.** Like benzene, with one CH replaced by N. Six π electrons (one from each ring atom), planar, aromatic. The nitrogen lone pair lies in an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring, outside the π system. Nitrogen is more electronegative than carbon, so it draws electron density from the ring (inductive and resonance effects); C-2, C-4 and C-6 become electron-poor.

### Basicity of pyridine

- Pyridine is a **moderately weak base (pKa about 5.2)**. It forms salts such as pyridinium chloride, and its lone pair is freely available because it is not part of the sextet.
- It is **much weaker than aliphatic amines** (piperidine about 11.1, triethylamine about 10.7). The lone pair is in an **sp2** orbital (33% s character) — held closer to the nucleus than an sp3 lone pair (25% s), so it is less available to a proton.
- It is **slightly stronger than aniline** (4.6), whose lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring.
- It is **much stronger than pyrrole**, whose lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet.
- **Effect of substituents**: electron-donating groups (methyl, amino at C-2/C-4) increase basicity (4-aminopyridine and 4-dimethylaminopyridine are much stronger bases); electron-withdrawing groups (nitro, halogen, cyano) decrease it.

### Synthesis

1. **Hantzsch pyridine synthesis** — two molecules of a β-ketoester (ethyl acetoacetate), one aldehyde and ammonia condense to give a **1,4-dihydropyridine**, which is oxidised (HNO3, or other oxidants) to the pyridine.

```text
 2 CH3COCH2COOEt + RCHO + NH3 ──► 1,4-dihydropyridine-3,5-dicarboxylate ──[O]──► pyridine
 (The 1,4-dihydropyridine stage is itself the core of nifedipine, amlodipine and
  felodipine — calcium channel blockers made by this very route.)
```

2. **Chichibabin pyridine synthesis (industrial)** — aldehydes (or ketones) heated with ammonia over a catalyst: acetaldehyde + formaldehyde + ammonia give pyridine and methylpyridines (picolines).
3. **From acetylene and hydrogen cyanide** — passed through a red-hot tube.
4. **From pentamethylenediamine** — heating its hydrochloride gives piperidine, which is dehydrogenated (e.g. with heat and a catalyst, or conc. H2SO4) to pyridine.

### Reactions of pyridine

**(a) Reactions at nitrogen (as a base and nucleophile)**

- With acids → pyridinium salts.
- With alkyl halides → N-alkylpyridinium salts (CH3I → N-methylpyridinium iodide).
- With acyl chlorides → N-acylpyridinium ions, which is why pyridine catalyses acylation.
- With SO3 → pyridine–SO3 complex (a mild sulphonating agent).
- With peracids (H2O2 in acetic acid, or perbenzoic acid) → **pyridine N-oxide**.

**(b) Electrophilic substitution — difficult, at C-3**

Pyridine reacts roughly a million times more slowly than benzene. The ring is electron-poor and, under the acidic conditions of nitration or sulphonation, the nitrogen is protonated to the even more deactivated pyridinium ion. Attack at C-3 is preferred because the intermediate from C-2 or C-4 attack would place a positive charge on the electronegative nitrogen.

| Reaction | Conditions | Product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nitration | KNO3 + fuming H2SO4, about 300 °C | 3-Nitropyridine (low yield) |
| Sulphonation | Oleum with HgSO4 catalyst, about 230–250 °C | Pyridine-3-sulphonic acid |
| Bromination | Br2 in oleum, about 130 °C | 3-Bromopyridine |
| Friedel–Crafts | Does not occur (N complexes the Lewis acid) | — |

**Pyridine N-oxide** is more reactive: the oxygen gives electrons back into the ring, so it nitrates at **C-4**. The oxygen can then be removed (e.g. with PCl3), giving 4-substituted pyridines.

**(c) Nucleophilic substitution — easy, at C-2 and C-4**

| Reaction | Reagent | Product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Chichibabin reaction** | Sodium amide (NaNH2) in toluene or liquid NH3, heat | 2-Aminopyridine (+ H2 lost as hydride) |
| With organolithium | Phenyllithium or butyllithium | 2-Phenyl- or 2-butylpyridine |
| With KOH | Fusion at about 300 °C | 2-Pyridone (2-hydroxypyridine) |
| Halide displacement | 2- or 4-chloropyridine + amines, alkoxides | Substituted pyridines |

Attack at C-2/C-4 is preferred because the negative charge in the intermediate can sit on the electronegative nitrogen.

**(d) Reduction** — sodium in ethanol, or H2 with Pt, gives **piperidine**.

**(e) Oxidation** — the ring resists oxidation, but alkyl side chains are oxidised to –COOH:

```text
 3-methylpyridine (β-picoline) ──KMnO4 / HNO3──► nicotinic acid (niacin, vitamin B3)
 4-methylpyridine (γ-picoline) ──[O]──► isonicotinic acid ──(ester + hydrazine)──► isoniazid
```

## 4.7 Quinoline (benzo[b]pyridine)

A benzene ring fused to the 2,3-bond of pyridine; nitrogen at position 1. Colourless oily liquid (bp about 238 °C), found in coal tar; first obtained by distilling quinine with alkali (hence the name). Weak base, pKa about 4.9.

```text
          5     4
       6 /\ ___/\ 3
         ||    ||          benzene ring (5–8) fused to pyridine ring (N-1 to C-4)
       7 \/‾‾‾‾\/ 2
          8     N 1
```

### Synthesis

1. **Skraup synthesis** — the classical method. Aniline is heated with glycerol, conc. H2SO4 and an oxidising agent (nitrobenzene; arsenic acid was also used); ferrous sulphate is added to moderate the otherwise violent reaction.

```text
 Step 1  glycerol ──conc. H2SO4 (−2 H2O)──► acrolein (CH2=CH–CHO)
 Step 2  aniline adds to the C=C of acrolein (Michael / 1,4-addition)
          → 3-anilinopropanal
 Step 3  acid-catalysed ring closure onto the benzene ring (ortho position), then loss of water
          → 1,2-dihydroquinoline
 Step 4  oxidation by nitrobenzene → quinoline
          (nitrobenzene is reduced to aniline, which can also react)
```

   Substituted anilines give substituted quinolines (p-toluidine → 6-methylquinoline).

2. **Doebner–Miller synthesis** — like Skraup, but an α,β-unsaturated aldehyde (or two aldehydes that form one by aldol) is used with HCl: aniline + crotonaldehyde → 2-methylquinoline (quinaldine).
3. **Friedländer synthesis** — o-aminobenzaldehyde (or o-aminoacetophenone) condenses with an aldehyde or ketone having an α-CH2 group in the presence of a base: o-aminobenzaldehyde + acetaldehyde → quinoline.
4. **Combes synthesis** — aniline + a 1,3-diketone (acetylacetone), then conc. H2SO4 → 2,4-dimethylquinoline.
5. **Conrad–Limpach synthesis** — aniline + a β-ketoester; the enamine formed is cyclised at high temperature to a 4-quinolone (4-hydroxyquinoline). Related routes give the 4-quinolone-3-carboxylic acid core of the fluoroquinolone antibiotics.

### Reactions

- **Electrophilic substitution in the benzene ring, at C-5 and C-8** (the pyridine ring is deactivated): nitration with HNO3/H2SO4 → mixture of 5- and 8-nitroquinoline; sulphonation with oleum → quinoline-8-sulphonic acid (and 5-isomer at different temperatures); bromination in the presence of acid → 5- and 8-bromo.
- **Nucleophilic substitution in the pyridine ring, at C-2 (and C-4)**: NaNH2 → 2-aminoquinoline; KOH fusion → 2-quinolone (carbostyril); organolithiums → 2-alkyl/aryl quinolines.
- **Oxidation** with alkaline KMnO4 destroys the benzene ring and gives **quinolinic acid** (pyridine-2,3-dicarboxylic acid) — showing that the pyridine ring is the more stable one.
- **Reduction**: tin and HCl, or mild catalytic hydrogenation, reduce the pyridine ring → 1,2,3,4-tetrahydroquinoline; vigorous hydrogenation → decahydroquinoline.
- **Basic reactions**: salts with acids, quaternary salts with alkyl halides, N-oxide with peracids.

## 4.8 Isoquinoline (benzo[c]pyridine)

Benzene fused to the 3,4-bond of pyridine; nitrogen at position 2. Colourless solid (mp about 26 °C), found in coal tar. Slightly stronger base than quinoline (pKa about 5.4).

### Synthesis

1. **Bischler–Napieralski synthesis** — an N-acyl derivative of β-phenylethylamine is cyclised with a dehydrating agent (POCl3, P2O5) to a **3,4-dihydroisoquinoline**, which is dehydrogenated (Pd, heat) to the isoquinoline.

```text
 C6H5–CH2–CH2–NH–CO–R  ──POCl3 / P2O5 (−H2O)──►  1-R-3,4-dihydroisoquinoline
 N-acyl-β-phenylethylamine                                │ Pd, heat (−H2)
                                                          ▼
                                                 1-R-isoquinoline
```

   Electron-donating groups (–OCH3) on the benzene ring help the ring closure; this route was used to make **papaverine**.

2. **Pictet–Spengler synthesis** — β-phenylethylamine condenses with an aldehyde (formaldehyde) in acid; the iminium ion cyclises to a **1,2,3,4-tetrahydroisoquinoline**. The same reaction makes many isoquinoline alkaloids in plants.
3. **Pomeranz–Fritsch synthesis** — benzaldehyde + aminoacetaldehyde diethyl acetal → Schiff base (benzalaminoacetal), which is cyclised by conc. H2SO4 → isoquinoline.

### Reactions

- **Electrophilic substitution at C-5** (some at C-8): nitration → mainly 5-nitroisoquinoline; sulphonation → 5-sulphonic acid.
- **Nucleophilic substitution at C-1** (the most reactive position): NaNH2 → 1-aminoisoquinoline; KOH → 1-isoquinolone.
- **Oxidation** with alkaline KMnO4 gives a mixture of **phthalic acid** and **cinchomeronic acid** (pyridine-3,4-dicarboxylic acid) — both rings can be attacked.
- **Reduction** (Sn/HCl or catalytic) → 1,2,3,4-tetrahydroisoquinoline.
- Salts, quaternary salts and N-oxides as for pyridine.

## 4.9 Acridine (dibenzo[b,e]pyridine)

Three fused six-membered rings — a pyridine ring in the middle of two benzene rings (the aza analogue of anthracene); nitrogen at position 10, the reactive carbon opposite it at **C-9**. Pale yellow crystalline solid from coal tar; weak base (pKa about 5.6); its dilute solutions fluoresce blue.

### Synthesis

1. **Bernthsen synthesis** — diphenylamine is heated with a carboxylic acid (or formic acid) and anhydrous zinc chloride at about 200–270 °C. Formic acid gives acridine; other acids give 9-substituted acridines (acetic acid → 9-methylacridine).
2. **From N-phenylanthranilic acid (via acridone)** — o-chlorobenzoic acid and aniline are coupled with copper (Ullmann reaction) to N-phenylanthranilic acid. Heating with conc. H2SO4 closes the ring to **acridone**; POCl3 converts it to **9-chloroacridine**, a key intermediate (9-chloroacridine + NH3 or amines → 9-aminoacridines).

### Reactions

- **Nucleophilic attack at C-9** — the most reactive site. Sodamide gives 9-aminoacridine; 9-chloroacridine exchanges Cl for amines, alkoxides and thiols easily.
- **Electrophilic substitution** occurs in the outer benzene rings, mainly at C-2 and C-7 (nitration, sulphonation).
- **Oxidation** with dichromate in acetic acid → acridone (C-9 becomes C=O).
- **Reduction** (Zn/HCl) → 9,10-dihydroacridine (acridan).
- Forms salts, quaternary salts and N-oxides.

## 4.10 Indole (benzo[b]pyrrole)

Benzene fused to the 2,3-bond of pyrrole; NH at position 1. Colourless solid (mp about 52 °C) with a faecal smell when concentrated (but floral when very dilute; used in perfumes). Found in coal tar and jasmine oil; part of the amino acid tryptophan.

```text
          4      3
       5 /\ ___/\         benzene ring fused to pyrrole ring;
         ||    ||  2      most reactive carbon = C-3
       6 \/‾‾‾‾\/
          7      N 1
                 H
```

### Synthesis

1. **Fischer indole synthesis** — the most important method. A phenylhydrazone of an aldehyde or ketone is heated with an acid catalyst (ZnCl2, polyphosphoric acid, BF3 or H2SO4).

```text
 C6H5–NH–NH2 + CH3COCH3 ──► acetone phenylhydrazone
          │ ZnCl2, heat
          ▼
 tautomerises to the ene-hydrazine
 → [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement (new C–C bond to the ortho carbon of the ring)
 → cyclisation and loss of NH3
 → 2-methylindole
```

   The carbonyl compound must have a CH2 (or CH3) group α to the C=O. Acetaldehyde does not work well, so indole itself is made from **pyruvic acid** phenylhydrazone → indole-2-carboxylic acid → heated (decarboxylation) → indole.

2. **Madelung synthesis** — an N-acyl-o-toluidine is heated strongly with a strong base (sodium amide or potassium tert-butoxide); intramolecular condensation gives a 2-substituted indole. N-formyl-o-toluidine gives indole itself.
3. **Reissert synthesis** — o-nitrotoluene condenses with diethyl oxalate (potassium ethoxide) to give ethyl o-nitrophenylpyruvate; reduction (Zn/acetic acid or Fe) turns –NO2 into –NH2, which cyclises onto the keto group → indole-2-carboxylic acid ester; hydrolysis and decarboxylation give indole.
4. **Bischler synthesis** — an α-haloketone (phenacyl bromide) heated with excess aniline gives a 2-arylindole.

### Reactions

- **Electrophilic substitution at C-3** (not C-2 as in pyrrole). Attack at C-3 gives an intermediate in which the positive charge is stabilised by nitrogen **without** disturbing the benzene ring's aromaticity; attack at C-2 would need to involve the benzene ring.

| Reaction | Reagent | Product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Formylation | DMF + POCl3 (Vilsmeier–Haack) | Indole-3-carbaldehyde |
| Mannich | HCHO + dimethylamine + acetic acid | Gramine (3-dimethylaminomethylindole), used to make tryptophan |
| Nitration | Benzoyl nitrate (non-acidic) | 3-Nitroindole |
| Halogenation | Mild reagents (e.g. N-bromosuccinimide) | 3-Haloindoles |
| Acylation | Acetic anhydride with heat | 3-Acetylindole (with some N-acetyl) |
| Michael addition | α,β-Unsaturated carbonyls | 3-Substituted indoles |

- If C-3 is occupied, substitution goes to C-2.
- **N–H acidity** — like pyrrole (pKa about 17); forms N-sodium or N-magnesium salts that can be alkylated.
- **Very weak base**; protonates on C-3 in strong acid and polymerises.
- **Reduction** with zinc and HCl, or catalytically, → indoline (2,3-dihydroindole).
- **Oxidation** — easily oxidised in air; controlled oxidation gives indoxyl, oxindole or isatin; ozone cleaves the 2,3-bond.

## 4.11 Pyrimidine (1,3-diazine)

Six-membered ring with nitrogens at 1 and 3. Colourless solid, very weak base (pKa about 1.3) because each nitrogen withdraws electrons from the other. Strongly π-deficient. It is the parent of three nucleic acid bases: **cytosine, thymine and uracil**.

```text
          4
       5 /\ N 3          N at 1 and 3; C-2, C-4 and C-6 lie between or next to
         ||  |           nitrogens (electron-poor, attacked by nucleophiles);
       6 \/\ 2           C-5 is the only position open to electrophiles
          N
          1
```

### Synthesis

The general **"principal synthesis"** joins a three-carbon unit (a 1,3-dicarbonyl compound — malonic ester, β-ketoester or β-diketone) with an N–C–N unit (urea, thiourea, guanidine or an amidine).

| Three-carbon unit | N–C–N unit | Product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diethyl malonate (sodium ethoxide) | Urea | **Barbituric acid** (pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione) |
| Diethyl phenylethylmalonate | Urea | Phenobarbital |
| Ethyl acetoacetate | Thiourea | 6-Methyl-2-thiouracil (antithyroid) |
| β-Diketone | Guanidine | 2-Aminopyrimidines |
| β-Diketone | Amidine | 2-Substituted pyrimidines (Pinner synthesis) |

```text
 CH2(COOEt)2  +  H2N–CO–NH2  ──NaOEt, heat──►  barbituric acid  +  2 EtOH
 diethyl malonate     urea
```

**Parent pyrimidine** — barbituric acid + POCl3 → 2,4,6-trichloropyrimidine; the chlorines are then removed by reduction (zinc dust in water, or catalytic H2/Pd) → pyrimidine.

### Reactions

- **Nucleophilic substitution** at C-2, C-4 and C-6 is easy when there is a leaving group: chloropyrimidines react with ammonia, amines, alkoxides and thiols (C-4 reacts before C-2). Chichibabin-type amination is also possible.
- **Electrophilic substitution** is very difficult in the parent ring; with two or more activating groups (–OH, –NH2) it occurs at **C-5**. Uracil brominates at C-5; this position is also where fluorine sits in 5-fluorouracil.
- **N-Alkylation** with alkyl halides (quaternisation at one nitrogen).
- **Tautomerism** — "hydroxypyrimidines" such as uracil and barbituric acid exist mainly in the keto (lactam) form.
- **Reduction** gives di- and tetrahydropyrimidines.

## 4.12 Purine (imidazo[4,5-d]pyrimidine)

A pyrimidine ring fused with an imidazole ring. Purine itself is a colourless solid, amphoteric (weak base, pKa about 2.4; weak acid, pKa about 8.9). The two nucleic acid bases **adenine** (6-aminopurine) and **guanine** (2-amino-6-oxopurine) are purines, as are uric acid, xanthine and caffeine. Purine uses a special numbering:

```text
          6
     1 N ╱ ╲ 5 ── N 7
       ‖     ‖      ╲
     2 ╲     ‖       8         pyrimidine ring: 1–6
       3 N ╲ ╱ 4 ── N 9        imidazole ring: 4, 5, 7, 8, 9
                     H
```

### Synthesis

1. **Traube purine synthesis** — the standard method. A **4,5-diaminopyrimidine** is heated with formic acid (or formamide, or ethyl orthoformate). The extra carbon closes the imidazole ring at C-8.

```text
 4,5-diaminopyrimidine  +  HCOOH  ──heat (−2 H2O)──►  purine
 2,4,5-triamino-6-hydroxypyrimidine + HCOOH ──►  guanine
 4,5-diamino-1,3-dimethyluracil  + HCOOH ──►  theophylline
```

   The diaminopyrimidine is made by the principal synthesis, nitrosation at C-5 and reduction of the nitroso group.

2. **Fischer's route from uric acid** — uric acid + POCl3 → 2,6,8-trichloropurine; the chlorines are replaced or removed stepwise (reduction with HI gives purine).

### Reactions

- **Nucleophilic substitution of chloropurines** — 6-chloropurine with thiourea or NaSH → **6-mercaptopurine**; with ammonia → adenine.
- **N-Alkylation** — methylation of xanthines: theophylline (1,3-dimethylxanthine) or theobromine (3,7-dimethylxanthine) + a methylating agent → **caffeine** (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine).
- **Electrophilic substitution at C-8** in activated purines (bromination of caffeine → 8-bromocaffeine).
- **Oxidation** — hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid (in the body by the enzyme xanthine oxidase; allopurinol blocks it).
- **Murexide test** — uric acid and caffeine evaporated with HNO3 (or H2O2/HCl) and then exposed to ammonia give a purple colour; used to identify purines.

## 4.13 Azepines and their derivatives

**Azepine** is a seven-membered ring with one nitrogen. The fully unsaturated 1H-azepine would have 8 π electrons (anti-aromatic if flat), so it is **non-planar (boat-shaped)**, non-aromatic and unstable; it behaves like a polyene. N-substituted azepines (N-ethoxycarbonyl) are more stable. Pharmaceutically important compounds are its **saturated or benzo-fused** derivatives, and the closely related **diazepines** (seven-membered rings with two nitrogens).

| Ring system | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Azepane (hexahydroazepine, fully saturated) | ε-Caprolactam (azepan-2-one) |
| Benzazepine | Benazepril, fenoldopam |
| Dibenz[b,f]azepine | Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine |
| 10,11-Dihydrodibenz[b,f]azepine (iminodibenzyl) | Imipramine, desipramine, clomipramine |
| 1,4-Benzodiazepine | Diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, lorazepam, alprazolam (triazolo-fused) |
| Dibenzodiazepine / thienobenzodiazepine | Clozapine, olanzapine |

### Synthesis

1. **1H-Azepines by ring expansion of benzene** — ethyl azidoformate (N3COOEt), on heating or irradiation, loses N2 to give a nitrene, which adds to benzene to form an azanorcaradiene; this opens (valence tautomerism) to **N-ethoxycarbonyl-1H-azepine**.
2. **ε-Caprolactam by Beckmann rearrangement** — cyclohexanone oxime + conc. H2SO4 → caprolactam (Unit 5). Caprolactam polymerises to nylon-6.
3. **Imipramine** — 2,2'-diaminobibenzyl is heated with acid; ring closure with loss of NH3 gives iminodibenzyl (10,11-dihydro-5H-dibenz[b,f]azepine). Its N–H is deprotonated with sodamide and alkylated with 3-chloro-N,N-dimethylpropylamine → **imipramine**.
4. **Carbamazepine** — iminostilbene (5H-dibenz[b,f]azepine) reacts with phosgene to give the N-carbonyl chloride, which with ammonia gives the carboxamide, **carbamazepine**.
5. **Diazepam (1,4-benzodiazepine)** — 2-amino-5-chlorobenzophenone is acylated with bromoacetyl bromide (or condensed with glycine ethyl ester); ammonia then closes the seven-membered ring to nordazepam, and N-methylation gives **diazepam**.

### Medicinal uses

| Drug | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Imipramine, clomipramine, desipramine | Tricyclic antidepressants |
| Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine | Antiepileptics; trigeminal neuralgia |
| Diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide | Anxiolytic, sedative, anticonvulsant (benzodiazepines) |
| Clozapine, olanzapine | Atypical antipsychotics |
| Benazepril | ACE inhibitor (benzazepinone) |

## Remember

- Azoles have one pyrrole-type and one pyridine-type N. Basicity: imidazole (7) > pyridine (5.2) > pyrazole ≈ thiazole (2.5) > oxazole (0.8) >> pyrrole.
- Pyrazole: 1,3-diketone + hydrazine; substitution at C-4. Imidazole: Debus–Radziszewski (glyoxal + HCHO + NH3); substitution at C-4/5. Oxazole: Robinson–Gabriel; Diels–Alder route to vitamin B6. Thiazole: Hantzsch (α-haloketone + thioamide/thiourea); substitution at C-5; thiamine is a thiazolium.
- Pyridine: Hantzsch (2 β-ketoester + aldehyde + NH3 → 1,4-dihydropyridine → oxidise). Electrophiles at C-3 (hard); nucleophiles at C-2/C-4 (Chichibabin: NaNH2 → 2-aminopyridine). N-oxide nitrates at C-4. pKa 5.2: weaker than piperidine (sp2 lone pair), stronger than aniline and pyrrole.
- Quinoline: Skraup (aniline + glycerol + H2SO4 + nitrobenzene; acrolein intermediate); E+ at C-5/C-8, Nu at C-2; KMnO4 → quinolinic acid.
- Isoquinoline: Bischler–Napieralski (N-acyl-β-phenylethylamine + POCl3), Pictet–Spengler, Pomeranz–Fritsch; E+ at C-5, Nu at C-1.
- Acridine: Bernthsen (diphenylamine + RCOOH + ZnCl2); C-9 most reactive; proflavine, mepacrine, amsacrine.
- Indole: Fischer (phenylhydrazone + acid, [3,3] shift, −NH3); E+ at **C-3**; tryptophan, serotonin, indomethacin, sumatriptan.
- Pyrimidine: 1,3-dicarbonyl + urea/thiourea/guanidine (barbituric acid from malonic ester + urea); Nu at 2/4/6, E+ only at 5.
- Purine: Traube (4,5-diaminopyrimidine + HCOOH); caffeine, theophylline, 6-mercaptopurine, acyclovir; murexide test.
- Azepines: non-planar 7-ring; drugs are dibenzazepines (imipramine, carbamazepine) and benzodiazepines (diazepam).
